cards.text: Pull up a stool, friend. Again the word of the LORD comes to Ezekiel the prophet, and God gives him a message to declare: "Wail, 'Alas for that day!'" When a message opens with WAIL, friend, that is not a birthday card.

cards.question: Ezekiel's message says that day is near. Which day is it?
True or false: God says this coming day will be a time of peace for the nations.

cards.text: Then the prophet gets specific: a sword is coming against Egypt. The slain fall, its wealth is taken away, and its foundations are torn down.

cards.question: When the slain fall in Egypt, there will be ___ in Cush.

cards.text: And Egypt doesn't fall alone: Cush, Put, Lud, Libya, all kinds of peoples and the men of the covenant land fall with her by the sword. It's like riding shotgun when your buddy gets pulled over, because guess who's ALSO sitting on the side of the road?

cards.question: Egypt's allies will fall, and God says her proud strength will ___.

cards.text: They fall by the sword from Migdol to Syene, one end of Egypt to the other. They'll be desolate among desolate lands, their cities lying among ruined cities.

cards.question: God says He will set fire to Egypt, and all her helpers will be shattered. When that happens, what will they know?

cards.text: On that day, God says, messengers will go out from Him in ships. Their destination: Cush.

cards.question: Why do God's messengers sail out to Cush?

answers.text: To frighten Cush out of complacency
To call Cush to come help Egypt
To carry off the wealth of Cush

cards.text: Frightened out of complacency, like dozing on the couch when your boss texts "Got a minute?" and suddenly you are WIDE awake. Anguish comes on the day of Egypt's doom, and God says, "For it is indeed coming."

cards.question: God says He will put an end to the hordes of Egypt by the hand of ___ king of Babylon.

cards.text: Nebuchadnezzar and his people are brought in to destroy the land. They draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain.

cards.question: True or false: God calls Nebuchadnezzar and his people the most ruthless of the nations.
God isn't done with Egypt's land yet. What does He say He'll do to its streams?

cards.text: He'll sell the land to the wicked and bring desolation by the hands of foreigners. Then He signs it: "I, the LORD, have spoken." Friend, that is NOT a rough draft.
The Lord GOD keeps going, and now He starts naming Egypt's cities one by one, beginning with Memphis.

cards.question: What does God say He will destroy in Memphis?
True or false: God says there will still be a prince in Egypt after this.

cards.text: Then comes a roll call of Egypt's cities: Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On and Pi-beseth, and not ONE of them gets good news. It's like a weather map where every single city in the country has the storm icon.
Then Tahpanhes. The day will be darkened there when God breaks the yoke of Egypt.

cards.question: When Egypt's proud strength comes to an end, a ___ will cover her.

cards.text: Her daughters will go into captivity. God sums it all up: He will execute judgment on Egypt, and they will know that He is the LORD.
Now a new date: the eleventh year, the seventh day of the first month. The word of the LORD comes to Ezekiel again, and this time it's about Pharaoh king of Egypt.

cards.question: God tells Ezekiel He has already broken something of Pharaoh's. What is it?
True or false: Pharaoh's broken arm has been bound up and splinted so he can hold the sword again.

cards.text: Not bound up, not splinted, like going to urgent care and walking out with a PAMPHLET. Then God says, "Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt."

cards.question: God says He will break Pharaoh's arms. Which ones?

answers.text: The strong one and the broken one
Only the one that is still strong

cards.question: God says He will make the ___ fall from Pharaoh's hand.

cards.text: On top of that, God will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.

cards.question: True or false: While Pharaoh's arms are broken, God strengthens the arms of Babylon's king.
God places a sword in the hand of Babylon's king. Whose sword is it?
True or false: God says Pharaoh will groan before Babylon's king like a mortally wounded man.

cards.text: Babylon's king gets stronger, Pharaoh's arms fall limp, and the king wields God's sword against the land of Egypt. Then that scattering line comes back: the Egyptians will be scattered throughout the lands, and they will know that He is the LORD.

findings.problem: "From Migdol to Syene, one end of Egypt to the other" adds a geographic fact that isn't in the passage text. Nothing in Ezekiel 30:6-7 says Migdol and Syene are Egypt's two ends, and the card gives no reference for that fact.

rule.text: Every fact and every verse number comes from that text. Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The question itself rules out two of the three answers. It says God will break Pharaoh's "arms," plural. That makes "Only the one already broken" and "Only the one that is still strong" impossible, so the right answer is given away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card calls Pathros, Zoan, Thebes and Pelusium "Egypt's cities." The text only calls On and Pi-beseth "those cities" (Ezekiel 30:17). Pathros is a region of Egypt, not a city. Card 1 of this stop says the same thing ("naming Egypt's cities one by one").

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "The sword of Goliath" doesn't match the other answers in kind or tone. It's a far-fetched throwaway that no baker would seriously consider for Babylon's king, so it reads as silly and makes the real choice a two-way pick.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Stop 2 opens with nearly the same pattern as Stop 1. Both go: story card, multiple choice, true or false, story card, then fill in the blank soon after.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Several story cards tell what God says will happen in plain present tense, as if it's happening in the passage. Examples: Stop 1 card 6 ("fall with her by the sword"), card 8 ("They fall by the sword"), card 14 ("are brought in to destroy the land") and Stop 2 card 18 ("Babylon's king gets stronger... wields God's sword"). The BSB gives all of these as future ("will"), and other cards keep "will." A baker could take a prophecy for a report of events.
findings.question: In prophetic passages, must story cards keep the text's future tense ("will") for what God says will happen? Or can Papa Dorin narrate predicted events in the present tense as storytelling?
